## Diagnosing the Open Circuit in a 2003 Impala Brake Light System

When a 2003 Chevy Impala loses its brake lights while retaining third brake light functionality, the fault usually lies within the pedal switch mechanism or the wiring harness leading to the rear cluster. The fact that you have verified all fuses and confirmed the bulbs are functional eliminates the most common power delivery issues, narrowing the investigation significantly. Since your high-mounted stop lamp (HMSL) activates correctly, we know the brake light switch is registering the pedal depression event; however, this specific architecture often suffers from an intermittent connection or a failure in the primary signal path that does not affect the auxiliary lamp.

The core issue typically stems from how the brake light switch interfaces with the vehicle's electrical ground and power distribution. In GM vehicles of this era, the brake light switch is a multi-function component. One terminal provides the trigger for the third brake light on the trunk lid, while a separate terminal or circuit handles the rear tail/brake lights. If the switch has an internal open circuit on the rear lighting side but remains functional for the high-mounted lamp, your symptoms align perfectly with this failure mode.

To isolate this without relying solely on visual inspection of the switch under the dash, you can use a multimeter to check for continuity between the switch terminals while applying pressure to the pedal. Disconnect the harness connector at the brake light switch and locate the pins corresponding to the rear brake lights (usually identified via a wiring diagram or by tracing the color code, often yellow/red combinations depending on the specific trim). Measure resistance across these pins while someone presses the brake pedal. If the resistance remains infinite or fluctuates without a stable low-ohm reading when the pedal is depressed, the switch assembly has failed internally and requires replacement.

Another frequent culprit in this specific vehicle model is corrosion at the connector mating surfaces within the trunk area or under the dashboard. Even if the fuse box appears intact, high-resistance connections can mimic a blown fuse. Inspect the wiring harness for signs of chafing against the firewall or suspension components, particularly near the rear wheel wells where the wiring loom passes. The 2003 Impala's rear hatch assembly can also introduce stress on the wiring loom connected to the third brake light; if this strain has compromised the main harness, it could potentially affect the primary circuit depending on the routing and connector design.

When replacing the brake light switch, ensure you purchase an OEM or high-quality aftermarket part that matches the specific mounting orientation of your model year. Generic switches may not align correctly with the pedal lever arm, leading to premature failure or inaccurate signal triggering. Before installing a new unit, clean the electrical contacts on the existing connector terminals. Using contact cleaner and a fine abrasive pad can restore conductivity if corrosion is the root cause rather than mechanical failure.

If you are comfortable working with vehicle diagnostics, consider using an OBD-II scanner that supports chassis control modules, though standard scanners often lack depth for simple lighting circuits. However, in many cases of this age and symptom profile, mechanical wear or internal switch failure is the definitive answer. The third brake light's operation confirms the switch logic board (if applicable) or the pedal lever is moving; the discrepancy indicates a dedicated circuit failure specific to the rear lamp cluster.
